setup.zh: 十月初十，子时，药园。你蹲在下风口的灵草丛后面，手里攥着一根萝卜。最里头那株紫玉参旁边，「咔、咔」两声。
setup.en: The tenth of the tenth month, midnight, the herb garden. You squat downwind behind a clump of herbs, a radish in your fist. By the purple jade ginseng at the far end: crack, crack.

recap.zh: 药园偷草的，是一只狰。它扑过来试你；你没下死手，放下一根萝卜。它吃了萝卜，在你脚边团成一团睡着了——小狰跟了你。
recap.en: The herb thief was a zheng. It came at you to try you; you didn't strike to kill, and laid down a radish. It ate the radish and curled up asleep at your feet — Little Zheng is yours.

zh: 五条尾巴，一只独角，一身赤红的毛。
偷来的，怎么吃都吃不饱；给的，一根就饱了。
en: The tenth of the tenth month, midnight, the herb garden.
Five tails, one horn, fur blazing red.
Stolen, never full; given, one is enough.

label.en: Open your hands, and set down the radish

exits.means: weathers the zheng's test without striking to kill, then gives it the radish; it joins him

withdrawn.zh: 小狰「咔、咔」两声，窜回了灵草丛里，又探出一只独角来。——再来。
withdrawn.en: Little Zheng goes crack, crack, darts back into the herbs, and pokes its one horn out again. — Again.

what.zh: 十月初八，周衡把药园巡夜交给了你；工钱是四分之一根蜡烛，和一句「记账」。
what.en: The eighth of the tenth month, Zhou Heng handed you the herb-garden night watch; the pay was a quarter candle and "on the books."

story.zh:
它吃完了一株，抬起鼻子，朝灯笼底下东角那一圈红线远远地嗅了一嗅——隔着半个园子，它也闻得出那里头什么都没有——打了个喷嚏，一脸嫌弃。它又去扒拉第二株。扒拉到一半，它停了下来，抬起头，鼻子朝西边抽了两抽。小满知道，它闻着了。下风口也不是十成十的，风有时候打个转，气味便漏过去了。它盯着他藏身的那丛灵草，身子往下一伏，五条尾巴一齐竖了起来，嘴里「咔、咔、咔」地响，这一回响得又急又硬，真像是有人拿石头在砸石头。

景阳冈上，武二郎打虎，凭的是一双拳头、十八碗酒。小满没有扑上去。他心口也跟着一紧，便让肚子一落，落得长长的，把那一紧按了下去，这才慢慢地站起身来，两只手摊开，让它瞧见他手里什么也没有——除了一根萝卜。他走了三步，停下来，弯下腰，把那根萝卜轻轻放在它面前的地上，然后退了回去，又蹲下了。

它停下嘴，看了看萝卜，又看了看他。

那个眼神，小满到老都记得。那眼神里有三层意思：头一层是「你在侮辱谁？」，第二层是「本兽吃的是灵草，一株值你一个月的灵石」，第三层——第三层他当时没看懂，后来才懂了，那一层是：「……这是给我的？」

它盯着萝卜看了很久很久。月亮往西边又挪了一截。

然后，它把萝卜吃了。

它吃萝卜，跟吃灵草不一样。吃灵草，它是抱着啃，啃一口，四下里张望一眼，像怕人抢；吃萝卜，它是趴在地上，两只前爪按着，一口一口，吃得很慢，连萝卜缨子都吃了。吃完了，它打了个嗝，这一声嗝，打得又长又响，「咔——」的一声，像敲了一记石磬。

然后它就地一歪，五条尾巴把自己团团围住，就这么睡着了——没跑，也没挪窝，当着一个生人的面。

小满蹲在那里，一动也不敢动。这东西偷了一年的灵草，一个月比一个月多，一株比一株值钱，可它越偷越饿。一根萝卜，不值一文钱，是人家给它的，它倒吃饱了，吃饱了便睡。他想起了马小宝睡着了还在食盒里摸的那一只手，只觉得心口有一点发凉。他把怀里那第二根萝卜掏出来，搁在它鼻子前头，留着，等它醒了吃。
story.en:
It finished one plant, lifted its nose and sniffed from afar at the ring of red thread in the east corner under the lantern — even across half the garden it could smell there was nothing in it — sneezed, and looked disgusted. It went back to paw at a second plant. Halfway through it stopped, lifted its head, and twitched its nose twice towards the west. Xiaoman knew it had caught him. Downwind is never a sure thing — the wind turns now and then and the scent slips through. It stared at the clump he was hiding behind, dropped low, all five tails straight up, its mouth going crk, crk, crk — hard and quick this time, just like someone smashing stone on stone.

On Jingyang Ridge, Wu Song killed his tiger with two fists and eighteen bowls of wine. Xiaoman didn't pounce. His own chest tightened too, so he let his belly fall, long and slow, and pressed the tightness down; only then did he stand up slowly, hands open, letting it see there was nothing in them — except a radish. He took three steps, stopped, bent, laid the radish gently on the ground in front of it, then backed away and squatted down again.

It stopped chewing, looked at the radish, then at him.

That look Xiaoman remembered into old age. It had three layers: the first, "Who do you think you're insulting?"; the second, "This beast eats spirit herbs — one of them is worth a month of your stones"; the third — the third he didn't understand at the time, only later: "…Is this for me?"

It stared at the radish a long, long time. The moon moved another stretch west.

Then it ate the radish.

It ate a radish differently from an herb. An herb it hugged and gnawed, a bite and a look all round, as if afraid of being robbed; the radish it ate lying down, both front paws pinning it, bite by bite, very slowly, leafy top and all. When it had finished it burped — a long, loud burp, "crrrack," like a stroke on a stone chime.

Then it toppled over where it lay, wrapped its five tails round itself, and went to sleep just like that — didn't run, didn't even shift its spot, right in front of a stranger.

Xiaoman squatted there, not daring to move. This thing had stolen herbs for a year, more each month, each plant dearer than the last — and the more it stole, the hungrier it got. A radish, worth not a copper, a gift — and it was full, and slept. He thought of Ma Xiaobao's hand still groping in the food box in his sleep, and felt something go cold in his chest. He took the second radish out of his coat and laid it in front of its nose, for when it woke.

story.zh:
萝卜是从伙房讨来的。小满傍晚去帮厨，削了一下午的萝卜，削完了，捧着一根，老老实实地对掌勺的胖大娘道：「大娘，我想要一根萝卜。」胖大娘瞧了瞧萝卜，又瞧了瞧他：「要萝卜干什么？」小满道：「练功。」胖大娘脸上的肉一抽一抽的，想笑又没笑出来，从筐里又拣了一根最大的，一齐塞进他怀里：「两根。练两遍。」

子时，药园。药园在后山的半腰上，背风向阳，三面是崖，一面是那道矮矮的石墙。园子里一畦一畦的灵草，叶子在夜里泛着一点幽幽的光，有绿的，有紫的，有白的，像一园子没点着的灯笼。小满在园子正当中寻了一块石头坐下，吸了一口气——那口气里的米粒，比他想的还要稠。他正要闭上眼睛，墙外头亮起了一盏灯笼。

灯笼后头是马小宝，身后跟着两个跟班，一人一只食盒。马小宝在墙头上探出半个身子，嚷道：「沈师弟！师兄来陪你巡夜！」也不等他答应，三个人便翻了进来，在园子门口的石阶上一坐，灯笼往中间一搁，食盒一开，桂花糕的甜香、腌肉的咸香，顺着风，飘了满园子。

小满道：「小宝哥，巡夜要静。」马小宝道：「静什么？贼听见有人，就不敢来了。这叫——」他咬了一口桂花糕，想了半天，「——打草惊蛇。」两个跟班一齐叫好。三个人吃了半夜，说了半夜，笑了半夜，还划了一回拳，输了的那个跟班，被罚去园子里「巡一圈」，提着灯笼绕着灵草畦子走了一遭，一路走一路唱，唱的是泗水上撑船人的小曲儿——他家就在泗水边上撑船：「泗水弯弯十八弯，哥哥撑篙妹摇船，摇到彭城换斗米，回头还有十八弯。」唱到「换斗米」，把自己唱笑了，又从头唱一遍，唱了三遍。丑时一过，三个人拍拍屁股走了，那盏灯笼和一只空食盒丢在石阶上，谁也没想起来拿。

小满蹲了一整夜，什么也没蹲着。天快亮的时候，他打着哈欠，把园子里一处一处看过去，看到园子最西头，哈欠便打不下去了：一株灵草，齐根没了。

那天上午，周衡在账簿上记了一笔：**十月初九，药园，丢一株。**他提着笔，看了小满一会儿，什么也没说，在页脚那一道底下，又画了一道。马小宝从执事房门口经过，把头伸进来，看了看那两道，笑眯眯地走了。

小满回到药园，蹲在那株灵草的断茬跟前。他爹不识字，可他认得山里每一种蹄印爪印，比他娘认字还认得准。被啃过的灵草，茬口齐齐的，是一口咬断的，不是扯断的，那东西牙口好。茬口旁边的泥地上，有几个小小的爪印，前头四个圆点，后头一个肉垫，猫儿大小，却比猫爪深，那东西身子沉。爪印边上，泥地上扫出一片扇形的印子，一道一道的，数一数，五道。

小满蹲在那片扇形的印子跟前，看了很久。五道。一条尾巴扫不出五道来，除非是五条尾巴。

他又在墙角的一块石头上，找到了一撮毛。红的，赤红赤红，比马小宝那件狐皮袄还红。

爪印是从西头的崖根底下来的，又回崖根底下去。昨夜那盏灯笼搁在东头，风从东边来，桂花糕、腌肉、三个人的汗味，一股脑儿顺着风往西边飘。那东西闻得见人，闻得见糕，就是闻不见园子正当中那块石头上一动不动的沈小满——人太多了。它便绕到了没人的那一头，吃了就走。

小满站起身来，拍了拍膝盖上的土。先看风，后看鹿。他爹的话，一句顶一句用。

第二夜，马小宝没有来——头一夜那一株，已经够他在周衡跟前说上一个月了。小满把马家丢下的那盏灯笼点上，连那只还剩着桂花糕渣的食盒，一并搁在园子东头的石阶上，自己绕到西头，在崖根底下风往园里灌的地方，一丛半人高的灵草后面蹲了下来。东头有灯、有糕味、有人味，那东西昨夜学乖了，今夜只会往没人的西头来——往他怀里来。他手里攥着一根萝卜，另一根揣在怀里，一动不动地蹲着，腰弯着，像老松底下那一截树桩子。用志不分。天地再大，他只认得脸上的风。蹲得两条腿都没了知觉，他也不挪。念头来了，他也不赶——他想起在黑松岭的那一回，他跟着他爹蹲鹿，蹲出了一个妖王，账上不知道该算赚了还是赔了。后来他算明白了：赚了。她吃了他一张饼，替他凿了一年的门，凿得自己薄成了一层纸。他摸了摸胸口的木牌，凉的。他小声道：「这回要是蹲着个什么，我先不急着出手。先看风。」

子时过了，丑时过了。园子东角那一尺见方的空地上，阿禾拿四根小竹签围了一圈，签上系着红线，线里头光秃秃的，什么也没有。忽听得「咔嚓」一声轻响，像是什么东西咬断了草茎。跟着，又是「咔、咔」两声，脆生生的，倒像是有人拿两块小石头在对着敲。他探出头去，只见药园最里头，那株最值钱的「紫玉参」旁边，蹲着一个东西。猫儿大小，一身赤红的毛，在月光底下红得发亮，身后拖着五条尾巴，一条一条，扫来扫去，扫得地上的泥一片一片的；头上生一只独角，短短的，尖尖的，像一截没长成的笋。它两只前爪抱着一株灵草，吃得咔嚓咔嚓直响，一边吃，一边往下掉渣，吃相实在难看得很。

小满胸口的木牌，这时候极轻地暖了一下，一个困得几乎听不清的声音，嫌弃地道：「……章莪之山的狰。五尾一角，其音如击石。《山海经》上都有……你们凡人，不念书的么……」便又没声了。原来那「咔、咔」两声，不是它在嚼，是它在叫——它一边吃，一边自己跟自己说话，说的大约是「好吃」，或者「还饿」。小满瞧着那一团，心想：书上的狰，是一只赤豹；眼前这一只，倒像一只吃撑了的红毛团子。
story.en:
The radish came from the kitchen. Xiaoman went to help there towards evening and peeled radishes all afternoon; when he'd finished he held one up and said honestly to the fat auntie at the stove: "Auntie, I'd like a radish." She looked at the radish, then at him. "What do you want a radish for?" "Practice," said Xiaoman. The flesh of her face twitched — wanting to laugh and not quite. She picked the biggest one out of the basket and pushed both into his coat. "Two. Practise twice."

Midnight. The herb garden. It lay halfway up the back mountain, out of the wind and facing the sun, cliffs on three sides and on the fourth that low stone wall. Inside, bed after bed of spirit herbs, their leaves giving off a faint glow at night — green, purple, white — like a garden of unlit lanterns. Xiaoman found a stone in the middle of the garden and sat, and drew a breath — there were more grains of rice in it than he'd hoped. He was about to close his eyes when a lantern lit up beyond the wall.

Behind the lantern was Ma Xiaobao, two hangers-on behind him, each with a food box. Ma Xiaobao leaned half over the wall and shouted: "Brother Shen! Your elder brother's come to keep you company on watch!" Without waiting for an answer the three of them climbed in, sat down on the steps by the garden gate, set the lantern between them and opened the boxes — the sweetness of osmanthus cake, the salt of cured pork, drifting on the wind all over the garden.

"Brother Xiaobao," said Xiaoman, "a night watch should be quiet." "Quiet what for?" said Ma Xiaobao. "A thief hears people, he won't dare come. That's called —" he bit his cake and thought a long while — "beating the grass to scare the snake." His two hangers-on applauded. The three of them ate half the night, talked half the night, laughed half the night, and played a round of finger-guessing; the loser was sentenced to "walk the round," and carried the lantern once round the herb beds singing a Si River boatman's ditty — his family poled boats on the Si: "The Si River bends eighteen bends, brother poles and sister rows; row to Pengcheng for a peck of rice, and back there's eighteen bends." At "a peck of rice" he made himself laugh, and started again from the top, three times over. Past the second watch the three of them dusted themselves off and left, the lantern and an empty food box forgotten on the steps.

Xiaoman squatted the whole night and caught nothing. Near dawn, yawning, he went round the garden bed by bed, and at the far west end he stopped yawning: one herb was gone, bitten off at the root.

That morning Zhou Heng wrote a line in the ledger: **Ninth day, tenth month. Herb garden, one lost.** Brush in hand he looked at Xiaoman a while, said nothing, and under the stroke at the foot of the page drew another. Ma Xiaobao, passing the office door, put his head in, looked at the two strokes, and went off all smiles.

Xiaoman went back to the garden and squatted by the stump of the herb. His father couldn't read, but he knew every hoofprint and pawprint on the mountain better than his mother knew her characters. The stalk was cut clean — bitten through in one bite, not torn; the thing had good teeth. On the mud beside it were a few small pawprints, four round dots in front and one pad behind, cat-sized but deeper than a cat's; the thing was heavy. Beside the prints, the mud had been swept into a fan, stroke after stroke — he counted: five.

Xiaoman crouched by that fan of marks a long time. Five. One tail can't sweep five lines — unless there are five tails.

On a stone in the corner by the wall he found a tuft of fur. Red — blazing red, redder than Ma Xiaobao's fox-fur jacket.

The prints came from the foot of the cliff at the west end, and went back there. Last night the lantern had stood at the east end with the wind blowing from the east, and osmanthus cake, cured pork and three men's sweat had all drifted west on it. The thing could smell people, could smell cake — what it couldn't smell was the motionless Shen Xiaoman on the stone in the middle of the garden: too many people. So it had gone round to the empty end, eaten, and left.

Xiaoman stood up and brushed the dirt off his knees. Watch the wind first, then the deer. Every one of his father's sayings earned its keep.

The second night Ma Xiaobao didn't come — last night's one plant would keep him talking in front of Zhou Heng for a month. Xiaoman lit the lantern the Ma boys had left, set it with the food box still smelling of cake on the steps at the east end, and went round to the west end himself, where the wind came down off the cliff into the garden, and squatted behind a clump of herbs half a man high. Light, cake and people at the east end: the thing had learned its lesson last night and would come only to the empty west end — straight to him. A radish in his hand, another in his coat, he squatted without moving, bent like the old stump under the pine. Undivided will. Heaven and earth might be vast; he knew only the wind on his face. His legs went numb; he didn't shift. Thoughts came and he didn't chase them off — he thought of the Black Pine Ridge, squatting for deer with his father and squatting up a demon queen instead; he still didn't know whether to book it as profit or loss. Later he worked it out: profit. She had eaten one flatbread of his and chiselled his gates for a year, chiselled herself thin as paper. He touched the token on his chest: cold. "If I catch something this time," he whispered, "I won't rush. Wind first."

Midnight passed, then the second watch. In the east corner of the garden, a patch one chi square had been fenced by A-He with four little bamboo pegs and a red thread; inside the thread was bare earth, nothing at all. Then — crack — a soft sound, like something biting through a stem. Then two more — crk, crk — crisp, like someone knocking two little stones together. He put his head out. At the far end of the garden, by the most valuable herb of all, the purple jade ginseng, crouched a creature. Cat-sized, all over red fur that shone in the moonlight, five tails behind it sweeping to and fro, sweeping the mud into patches; on its head a single horn, short and sharp, like a bamboo shoot that hadn't grown. It held an herb in both front paws and crunched away, dropping bits as it ate — truly dreadful table manners.

Just then the token on Xiaoman's chest went faintly warm, and a voice so sleepy he could barely hear it said, with disgust: "…A zheng, from Mount Zhang'e. Five tails, one horn, cry like stone striking stone. It's all in the *Classic of Mountains and Seas*… don't you mortals read?" Then nothing more. So the two crk, crk weren't chewing but calling — it was talking to itself as it ate, probably saying "tasty," or "still hungry." Xiaoman looked at the bundle and thought: the zheng in the book is a red leopard; this one looks more like an overstuffed red furball.
